fetched_contents.text: Americans’ Perceptions About Immigrants from Different World Regions: Evidence from a Multinomial Conjoint Experiment | Journal of Experimental Political Science Abstract The literature in political science considers (sometimes inaccurate) perceptions of immigrants as a factor in anti-immigration attitudes among natives, but much less is known about perceptions regarding immigrants from specific regions. In this paper, I explore Americans’ perceptions about immigrants from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East. To measure these perceptions, I apply a conjoint experiment with a multinomial outcome, in which respondents are asked to categorize hypothetical immigrants as coming from one of the five regions. Results from a nationally diverse sample demonstrate that immigrants from all regions other than Europe are associated with speaking poor English. Immigrants from Latin America are also associated with welfare dependency and rule-breaking behavior, while the opposite is true for immigrants from Asia. These negative perceptions may at least partly explain opposition to non-European, and specifically Latin American, immigration in the United States. One important factor that underlies political conflict around immigration concerns the ways in which natives perceive immigrants, with perceptions not necessarily reflecting the reality. Indeed, immigrants are often seen as poorer, less educated, and more culturally distant than they are (for a review, see Lutz and Bitschnau Reference Lutz and Bitschnau2022). Since all these attributes are usually seen by natives as undesirable for potential immigrants (Hainmueller and Hopkins Reference Hainmueller and Hopkins2015; Valentino et al. Reference Valentino, Soroka, Iyengar, Aalberg, Duch, Fraile, Hahn, Hansen, Harell, Helbling, Jackman and Kobayashi2019), negative perceptions are politically consequential. Existing studies show that variance in perceptions about immigrants – concerning their reasons for migrating, employment, and legality – predicts attitudes toward immigration (Blinder Reference Blinder2015; Zhirkov Reference Zhirkov2021b). The same logic should extend onto specific immigrant origins: natives likely form distinct perceptions about immigration from different countries and regions. These origin-specific perceptions have not yet received enough attention in the literature, but they have important implications for immigration policy opinions and anti-immigrant prejudice. If immigrants from some regions are seen as having desirable characteristics, whereas immigrants from other regions are believed to have undesirable ones, it can explain the presence of systematic discrimination against certain origins (Newman and Malhotra Reference Newman and Malhotra2018; Zhirkov Reference Zhirkov2021a). Support for restrictive policies and stricter enforcement can be higher if immigration is seen as coming primarily from regions associated with undesirable attributes. In the present paper, I address this gap by exploring Americans’ perceptions about immigrants from different world regions. In an original conjoint task with a multinomial outcome, I present respondents with profiles of hypothetical immigrants and ask them to guess whether each immigrant came from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, or the Middle East. Results of the experiment demonstrate that immigrants from all world regions other than Europe are associated with poor English skills. Perceptions about immigrants from Latin America are particularly negative: they include welfare dependency and rule-breaking behavior. Immigrants from Asia, on the contrary, are seen as self-sufficient and law-abiding. Positive perceptions about European immigrants are exhibited by both white and nonwhite respondents, although they are somewhat weaker among the latter. Overall, these results show that Americans’ opposition to non-European immigration, and Latin American immigration in particular, may stem from negative perceptions. Methodologically, my analysis demonstrates how conjoint experiments with multinomial outcomes can help to answer important questions in political science. Measuring perceptions about immigrant origins Influential experimental studies suggest that Americans, as well as citizens of other industrial democracies, have broadly meritocratic preferences on immigration: they are ready to admit immigrants who have valuable skills, speak good English, and follow the rules – whereas country of origin has little effect (Hainmueller and Hopkins Reference Hainmueller and Hopkins2015; Valentino et al. Reference Valentino, Soroka, Iyengar, Aalberg, Duch, Fraile, Hahn, Hansen, Harell, Helbling, Jackman and Kobayashi2019). At the same time, there is no agreement in the literature regarding both absolute and relative role of origin in attitudes toward immigration. Indeed, Americans seem to differentiate between more and less desirable immigrant groups (Zhirkov Reference Zhirkov2021a). Most prominently, attitudes toward Hispanics impact whites’ opinions on immigration, and featuring immigrants from Latin America in the media boosts nativism (Brader, Valentino, and Suhay Reference Brader, Valentino and Suhay2008; Branton et al. Reference Branton, Cassese, Jones and Westerland2011; Valentino, Brader, and Jardina Reference Valentino, Brader and Jardina2013). According to more recent evidence, immigrants from the Middle East can be another group that provokes particularly strong opposition (Konitzer et al. Reference Konitzer, Iyengar, Valentino, Soroka and Duch2019). The core logic is that respondents are asked to choose among profiles that vary across attributes, and their choices reveal the relative value they assign to each attribute and level [N1-R2][N1-R3]. In immigration research, this means respondents are shown hypothetical immigrants with different combinations of race/ethnicity, country of origin, education, language skills, and other attributes, and asked to rank, choose, or otherwise indicate which profiles are more or less desirable [N2-R5][N2-F1].

A key step in the design is coding and normalizing attribute levels. The evidence shows that conjoint experiments break a product or service into attributes and levels, then test different combinations [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In the immigration context, attributes such as gender, education, employment plans, job experience, profession, language skills, and country of origin are explicitly included as features to be varied [N2-R5]. The randomization and experimental design also matter because they allow researchers to disentangle correlated attributes such as language skills and country of origin [N2-R3]. That implies normalization is not just arbitrary coding; it is part of the design to ensure attribute effects can be measured separately and meaningfully.

Statistical estimation is the other main mechanism. The evidence states that conjoint analysis uses statistical analysis to compute mathematical representations of survey respondents' preferences for product features [N1-R3][N1-R5]. In the cited immigration studies, this involves multinomial or choice-based estimation: one study uses a multinomial conjoint experiment in which respondents categorize immigrants by region [N2-F1], while others use standard conjoint methods with attribute levels and choice tasks [N2-R5]. The broader literature also emphasizes that conjoint analysis is used to assess the direction and strength of citizens' preferences [N4-R5]. So, the statistical methods typically include maximum likelihood, logit, or mixed-effects models, and they yield preference parameters that quantify how much each attribute level contributes to the likelihood of being chosen or preferred [N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-R5].

Overall, conjoint experiments translate descriptive attributes into preference estimates by letting respondents trade off attributes in choice tasks, coding and normalizing attribute levels to separate effects, and using statistical methods to estimate how much each attribute matters to preference [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5][N2-R5].

### 1) How conjoint experiments translate descriptive attributes into preference estimates

The evidence also emphasizes that randomization helps researchers disentangle correlated attributes such as language skills and country of origin [N2-R3]. That is important because it means the experiment is not just measuring one attribute in isolation; it is trying to estimate how attributes interact and how respondents normalize them in trade-offs.

The statistical estimation step is equally important. The evidence states that conjoint analysis uses statistical analysis to compute mathematical representations of survey respondents’ preferences for product features [N1-R3][N1-R5]. In immigration research, this often takes the form of multinomial conjoint experiments or standard choice-based conjoint methods [N2-F1][N2-R5]. The broader literature also notes that conjoint analysis is used to assess the direction and strength of citizens’ preferences [N4-R5]. Together, these methods yield preference parameters that quantify how much each attribute level contributes to preference, allowing researchers to compare the relative importance of education, language skills, country of origin, and other attributes [N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-R5].

### 5) Bottom line: why conjoint experiments matter for understanding immigration preferences

Conjoint experiments help us understand public preferences for immigrants by descriptive attributes because they:

1. **Let respondents trade off attributes** in choice tasks, revealing the relative value they attach to each attribute level [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-R5].
2. **Code and normalize attributes** to separate effects and disentangle correlated attributes such as language skills and country of origin [N1-R4][N2-R3].
3. **Estimate preference parameters** statistically, allowing researchers to compare how education, language skills, country of origin, and other attributes influence choice [N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-R5].
4. **Identify which attributes drive preference differences**, especially education, language skills, country of origin, and race/ethnicity [N2-R1][N2-R5][N2-F1][N5-R3].

It further states that variance in perceptions about immigrants predicts attitudes toward immigration, and that origin-specific perceptions have important implications for immigration policy opinions and anti-immigrant prejudice [N2-F1]. This is a key point: conjoint results do not exist in isolation. They inform how people think about immigration in ways that can influence support for restrictive policies, enforcement preferences, and broader nativist sentiment [N2-F1]. The same paper also notes that existing studies show perceptions about immigrants’ reasons for migrating, employment, and legality predict immigration attitudes, and that the same logic should extend to specific immigrant origins [N2-F1]. So conjoint evidence helps explain not just what people prefer, but why those preferences may translate into policy support.

Findings also vary by country and survey context. The evidence is strongest for the United States, where the conjoint experiment explicitly uses a multinomial outcome with a nationally diverse sample [N2-F1]. In contrast, the broader literature cited in the study notes that research on perceptions about immigrants vs. natives exists, but perceptions about immigrants from specific countries or regions are usually not directly measured [N2-F1]. This suggests that the evidence is more abundant and directly comparable for U.S. respondents than for other countries, and that findings may differ when studies are conducted in different contexts. The study also notes that Americans seem to differentiate between more and less desirable immigrant groups, and that attitudes toward Hispanics impact whites’ opinions on immigration [N2-F1]. This implies that context matters because the attributes and their meanings may not be universally interpreted the same way across societies.

### 4) How attribute interaction and validity concerns affect interpretation

Attribute interaction and validity concerns significantly affect interpretation of conjoint results. The evidence shows that researchers often explicitly estimate interactions to separate correlated attributes. In immigration research, the design is described as useful because it can disentangle correlated attributes such as language skills and country of origin [N2-R3]. This means that attribute interactions are estimated and matter because they allow researchers to distinguish whether a preference is driven by one attribute alone or by the combination of attributes. The same study also reports that immigrants from different regions are associated with different combinations of undesirable or desirable attributes, which reinforces that interactions are important for understanding how profiles are evaluated together [N2-F1]. In other words, attribute interactions can change the meaning of a result: a given level of education may be more or less valuable depending on country of origin or other attributes in the profile.

Validity threats such as measurement error or response bias can change conclusions. The evidence from the validity literature is broad: conjoint analysis is described as a method of measurement that allows researchers to assess the direction and strength of citizens’ preferences [N4-R5]. However, validity concerns are also explicitly discussed. The PNAS study compares results from conjoint and vignette analyses on which immigrant attributes generate support for naturalization, suggesting that validity threats should be addressed by comparing methods [N4-R2]. In addition, the evidence notes that conjoint analysis has become popular among social scientists for measuring multidimensional preferences, but it also points to limitations and validity concerns in the broader conjoint literature [N4-R3]. More directly, the evidence on measurement error states that sign violations occur because of errors in the conjoint analysis method, and that sources of these errors are discussed [N6-R4]. This implies that if respondents misinterpret attributes, if the attribute levels are not well defined, or if the design is flawed, the estimated preference parameters can be unreliable.

Remedies used to improve estimation and inference include careful design, comparison with other methods, and explicit attention to sign constraints. The evidence supports this by showing that conjoint experiments are often used with multinomial or choice tasks that randomize profiles and separate attributes [N2-F1][N2-R3]. The PNAS comparison of conjoint and vignette results is one remedy for validity concerns, because it provides a benchmark against which conjoint findings can be checked [N4-R2]. The broader literature also emphasizes that conjoint analysis uses statistical analysis to compute preference parameters and that its methods are used to estimate and interpret citizens’ preferences [N1-R3][N4-R5]. In addition, the evidence on attribute interaction suggests that researchers should estimate interaction effects when relevant, because correlated attributes can obscure the true preference structure [N2-R3]. The validity discussion also implies that researchers should be cautious about measurement error and response bias, and that sign violations can be addressed by discussing the sources of error and using a priori sign constraints [N6-R4].

### 5) Bottom line: why conjoint experiments matter for understanding immigration preferences

Conjoint experiments help us understand public preferences for immigrants by descriptive attributes because they:

1. **Let respondents trade off attributes** in choice tasks, revealing the relative value they attach to each attribute level [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-R5].
2. **Code and normalize attributes** to separate effects and disentangle correlated attributes such as language skills and country of origin [N1-R4][N2-R3].
3. **Estimate preference parameters** statistically, allowing researchers to compare how education, language skills, country of origin, and other attributes influence choice [N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-R5].
4. **Identify which attributes drive preference differences**, especially education, language skills, country of origin, and race/ethnicity [N2-R1][N2-R5][N2-F1][N5-R3].
5. **Show how preferences change with attribute combinations**, because interactions matter and profiles are evaluated together [N2-R3][N2-F1].
6. **Link preferences to real-world policy outcomes**, showing that perceptions can explain opposition to certain immigrant groups and influence immigration attitudes [N2-F1].
7. **Vary by country and survey context**, with stronger evidence in the United States and broader implications for other settings [N2-F1].
8. **Require careful handling of validity concerns**, because measurement error, response bias, and interaction effects can change conclusions [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

In other words, conjoint experiments do not just measure preferences; they do so in a way that makes the underlying attributes and their interactions visible. That makes them uniquely useful for understanding public attitudes toward immigration, especially when the goal is to distinguish between race/ethnicity, country of origin, education, language skills, and other descriptive attributes.
